/-!
# Erdős Problem 397

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/397](https://www.erdosproblems.com/397)
- [MathOverflow] (https://mathoverflow.net/questions/138209/product-of-central-binomial-coefficients)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Nat

namespace Erdos397

/--
Are there only finitely many solutions to
$$
  \prod_i \binom{2m_i}{m_i}=\prod_j \binom{2n_j}{n_j}
$$
with the $m_i,n_j$ distinct?

Somani, using ChatGPT, has given a negative answer. In fact, for any $a\geq 2$, if $c=8a^2+8a+1$,
$\binom{2a}{a}\binom{4a+4}{2a+2}\binom{2c}{c}= \binom{2a+2}{a+1}\binom{4a}{2a}\binom{2c+2}{c+1}.$
Further families of solutions are given in the comments by SharkyKesa.

This was earlier asked about in a [MathOverflow] question, in response to which Elkies also gave an
alternative construction which produces solutions - at the moment it is not clear whether Elkies'
argument gives infinitely many solutions (although Bloom believes that it can).

This was formalized in Lean by Wu using Aristotle.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11,
formal_proof using lean4 at "https://gist.githubusercontent.com/llllvvuu/40d68cfa9de9f43eece07ff4fdc3b0ef/raw/966750065320fe126fbe5a8a7ea50439d7519c6c/397.lean",
formal_proof using formal_conjectures at "https://github.com/XC0R/formal-conjectures/blob/3c356a50a21bcbf3543f960b0c92d7fb26228cb6/FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/397.lean#L147"]
theorem erdos_397 :
    answer(False) ↔
      {(M, N) : Finset ℕ × Finset ℕ | Disjoint M N ∧
      ∏ i ∈ M, centralBinom i = ∏ j ∈ N, centralBinom j}.Finite := by
  sorry

end Erdos397

reformulations.difference: The source asks about solutions of ∏_i C(2m_i, m_i) = ∏_j C(2n_j, n_j) "with the m_i, n_j distinct", implicitly over positive integers. The Lean statement counts ordered pairs (M, N) of `Finset ℕ` with `Disjoint M N` and equal products of `Nat.centralBinom`. So index 0 is allowed (`centralBinom 0 = 1`), which admits the trivial solutions (∅, ∅), ({0}, ∅) and (∅, {0}). Also, a solution is a pair of sets rather than a pair of indexed families.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: "All m_i, n_j distinct" means no index repeats within a side and none is shared between sides. That is exactly two finite sets that are disjoint, so `Finset` plus `Disjoint` encodes it. The forum reads it the same way ("we require m_i, n_j distinct, which corresponds to a_m ∈ {0, ±1}"). Ordered pairs vs. indexed families: each pair of sets has finitely many orderings, so finiteness is unaffected. Index 0: removing 0 from both sides maps the Lean solution set S onto the set S⁺ of positive-integer solutions. Disjointness and the products are preserved because C(0,0) = 1. Each fibre has at most 3 elements (0 in M, 0 in N, or neither; not both, by disjointness). So S ⊆ image of S⁺ × Fin 3 and S⁺ ⊆ S, hence S is finite iff S⁺ is finite. Enumerating all pairs inside {0,…,7} in Lean finds only the three trivial solutions, so nothing spurious appears. I proved `(False ↔ S.Finite) ↔ (False ↔ {(M,N) | (∀ m ∈ M, 0 < m) ∧ (∀ n ∈ N, 0 < n) ∧ Disjoint M N ∧ ∏ = ∏}.Finite)` in Lean; it depends only on propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound.

review.notes:
The file has one declaration. `answer(False) ↔ {(M, N) | Disjoint M N ∧ ∏ M centralBinom = ∏ N centralBinom}.Finite` elaborates to `False ↔ S.Finite`, i.e. S is infinite. That is the negative answer to erdosproblems.com's \"Are there only finitely many solutions … with the m_i, n_j distinct?\". The site records it as \"DISPROVED (LEAN)\", so the category (`research solved`) and the answer are consistent with the source and there is no status issue. The docstring reproduces the site's LaTeX text verbatim, except \"I believe\" became \"Bloom believes\". The MathOverflow question adds constraints (the same number of terms on each side and ∑x_i = ∑y_i) that are not in the Erdős–Graham/erdosproblems version; Tao says so in the forum. The file rightly omits them.

Checks run: in /workspace/review/proof.lean I proved the repository's exact statement (definitional equality with `type_of% Erdos397.erdos_397` checked by `rfl`) in about 60 lines, via Somani's family: for a ≥ 2, c = 8a²+8a+1, M = {a, 2a+2, c}, N = {a+1, 2a, c+1}. Only the standard axioms are used. This is expected for a solved problem, and the proof is the source's own solution. With `#eval` I confirmed the family for small a (and that it degenerates at a = 1, as the source's a ≥ 2 anticipates), Elkies' distinct examples, SharkyKesa's unequal-size solution {5,7,19} vs {1,2,3,6,20}, and octonion's family.

The `lean4` gist has no `sorry`. It proves `Set.Infinite {s : List ℕ × List ℕ | (s.1 ++ s.2).Nodup ∧ products equal}`, which is equivalent up to reordering. It targets Lean v4.24.0, so I read it but did not compile it here.

I could not obtain the original Erdős–Graham (1980) monograph text for p. 77. Faithfulness was judged against the cited erdosproblems.com statement.
